Among valid disclosures, intc_2024_7_D026 (Network and Edge) discusses moving networks to software infrastructure with AI-enabled compute/connectivity solutions for the edge, and intc_2024_7_D028 (Network and Edge) details the development of high-performance AI-enabled compute platforms and edge-optimized AI-enabled platforms based on Xeon/Core/Atom silicon. comparisons.peer_topic: Adaptive Computing and Embedded Systems Portfolio Expansion
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD expanded its adaptive computing portfolio with the launch of Versal Series Gen 2 devices, including Versal AI Edge and Prime Series Gen 2 adaptive SoCs, which integrate preprocessing, AI inference, and postprocessing for end-to-end acceleration of AI-driven embedded systems.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and AMD disclose strategies to expand their portfolios for AI-enabled computing at the edge using specific hardware platforms. Intel focuses on delivering 'edge-optimized AI-enabled platforms' based on its Xeon, Core, and Atom processors to help customers process data faster at the edge (intc_2024_7_P031_S001). Similarly, AMD expanded its adaptive computing portfolio with Versal Series Gen 2 devices, specifically the 'Versal AI Edge Series Gen 2,' which integrates preprocessing, AI inference, and postprocessing for 'end-to-end acceleration of AI-driven embedded systems' (amd_2024_7_P006_S001). Both companies are actively developing specialized silicon for edge AI workloads.

sentences.text: We deliver edge-optimized AI-enabled platforms for edge applications based on our Intel Xeon, Intel Core, and Intel Atom® processor portfolio, which reduces operational complexity for our customers and helps our customers create, store, and process data at the edge so they can analyze it faster and act on it sooner.

We expanded our adaptive computing portfolio with differentiated solutions with the launch of the new Versal™ Series Gen 2 devices, including the new Versal AI Edge Series Gen 2 and Versal Prime Series Gen 2 adaptive SoCs, which bring preprocessing, AI inference, and postprocessing together in a single device for end-to-end acceleration of AI-driven embedded systems.

peer_results.rationale: While Avago mentions infrastructure software for 'edge' platforms (avgo_2024_7_P003_S004), its primary disclosure candidate avgo_2024_7_D001 focuses on a broad portfolio of semiconductors for data center and enterprise networking (including AI networking) rather than specific on-premises edge AI compute platforms comparable to Intel's Xeon/Atom-based solution. The 'edge' reference in avgo_2024_7_P003_S004 is part of a generic list of cloud/platform types for software solutions, lacking the specific hardware platform and edge optimization context found in Intel's disclosure.

Micron's disclosures focus on memory manufacturing capacity, wafer starts, and revenue declines driven by DRAM/NAND market conditions. There is no comparable disclosure regarding AI-enabled edge computing platforms or silicon solutions for edge data processing.

NVIDIA's disclosures focus on accelerated computing for data centers, AI training (LLMs), and new services like DGX Cloud. While NVIDIA has edge products, the provided candidate sentences (nvda_2024_7_D002, nvda_2024_7_D008) describe high-performance data center AI and demand risks for generative AI, which is distinct from Intel's specific focus on on-premises edge AI platforms for industries like retail and healthcare using CPU-based architectures.

Qualcomm's disclosures focus on 5G technology, on-device AI for mobile handsets, automotive, and IoT, driven by smartphone adoption. While QCOM mentions 'on-device artificial intelligence' in automotive/IoT (qcom_2024_7_P026_S001), this differs from Intel's on-premises edge computing platforms designed for industrial and enterprise data processing at the network edge rather than device-side connectivity and mobile applications.
